steps.instruction: Define canonical records as the single source of truth for a repeating workflow: identify which data—customer details, invoices, orders, or support tickets—must match across systems and which mismatches currently cause rework or decision delays.

Estimate the weekly time cost of reconciling or re-entering data across tools, and note whether the owner re-approves decisions because records conflict—this threshold determines whether automation saves hours or solves a coordination problem.
Map the workflow: document the manual entry points, which tool holds the current truth for each field, and where decisions are blocked or duplicated because records diverge.

Decide whether the constraint is technical (data format, API availability, tool limits) or organizational (approval chain, data ownership, human review gates)—canonical-record design differs for each.

Assess whether AI automation fits: if records are semi-structured text (invoices, emails, chat logs), extraction and verification automation is a candidate; if records are already structured and synchronized, the work is lower-level integration, not AI.

Schedule a free 30-minute diagnostic call to review the workflow, confirm the canonical-record bottleneck, and decide on a fixed-price pilot scope and success measures; human approval remains with the owner throughout.

constraints_to_preserve.handling: Do not invent customer results, outcomes, or capabilities; describe only the decision framework and self-built demo features where relevant.
Require human approval for all data-integrity decisions and money movement; exclude high-sensitivity or bulk-automation workflows.
Maintain the frozen persona voice, approved evidence status, and founder-to-founder trust-first approach; no CTAs or fabricated urgency.
Use plain English; keep the workflow analysis distinct from the automation proposal; treat the diagnostic as the factual next step, not a guarantee.
